1:
The psalm carries no title, and two of them draw opposite conclusions from the same evidence. John Calvin observes that although the inscription is wanting, the ancient versions and the apostle in the epistle ascribe the psalm to David, so that there can be no doubt whose composition it is. Adam Clarke lists the same versions and the same apostolic quotation, and then sets it aside: eminent critics believe the psalm composed during the captivity, and the apostle only followed the common opinion in quoting it as David’s, because the Psalter in general was attributed to him. He adds that nine manuscripts write the psalm as part of the one preceding, though it must certainly have been an ode by itself since the subject is widely different, and reports a division of it into three speaking parts, the people, then the priest or prophet, then God himself. Keil and Delitzsch mark the same break from the other side, observing that a second stanza begins in the middle of the seventh verse, where the voice of God meets the assembly, admonishing, out of the sanctuary.

How the praise is to be offered occupies the rest. Augustine of Hippo hears in the opening a call to a great banquet of joy, and notes that since there is a wicked joy as well as a righteous one it was not enough to say let us rejoice, the psalm distinguishing it briefly by adding in the Lord. John Calvin presses the verb rather than the mood: the word means to make haste, and the psalmist calls them to speed into God’s presence because we are naturally backward when summoned to thanksgiving; he adds that the outward worship of God consisted principally in the sacrifice of praise and not in dead ceremonies. Charles Ellicott contrasts the general invitation here with the heathen warning that bade the uninitiated keep far off, and remarks that no one English expression carries the full burst of instrumental and vocal music meant by the word rendered a joyful noise. Matthew Henry insists on the body as well as the voice, since although bodily exercise alone profits little it is our duty to glorify God with our bodies; and he adds that we do not want matter for praise, but it were well if we did not want a heart. C.H. Spurgeon turns the same point into a warning that very much even of religious singing is offered not to the Lord but to the ear of the congregation. Adam Clarke reads the thanksgiving as a confession-offering, without which no acknowledgment of sin is acceptable, and finds three divine names in the third verse, one implying strength, one being and essence, and one covenant relation to mankind.

The strength of the hills is a hard word and both critics say so. Charles Ellicott notes that it occurs only here and in three other places, that the root usually assigned to it means to be weary, so that the sense of strength can be got from it only by deriving a word from its opposite, and offers two ways out: keeping that derivation, mines or treasures, because of the labour of extracting metal; or, with the old versions, heights, and by another derivation shining, so that the phrase means sunny summits and the rhythm is preserved by an antithetic parallelism. Keil and Delitzsch reject the mining sense on exactly that ground, since the clause is to all appearance meant as the antithesis of the shafts of the earth, and object that the derivation from weariness will not serve, fatigues and indefatigableness being notions that lie very wide apart. John Gill keeps to depths so deep that only God can penetrate them, John Wesley to the strongest or highest mountains, and Adam Clarke to the plain contrast that the greatest deeps are fathomed and the greatest heights accessible to him.
6:
The three verbs of the renewed summons are taken as three distinct acts by one and as one act by another. Adam Clarke separates them: the first is to prostrate ourselves, the highest act by which the supremacy of God is acknowledged; the second is to crouch or cower down with the legs bent under, as a dog in the presence of his master, waiting solicitously to receive his commands; the third is to put the knees to the ground in the posture of those who supplicate. Charles Ellicott agrees that the first word properly means to prostrate oneself, and adds that kneeling low in the east is used only in moments of deep humiliation and is not mentioned at all until late. C.H. Spurgeon allows the body its part without making it everything: posture is not all, and prayer is heard when knees cannot bend, yet it is seemly that an adoring heart should show its awe by prostrating the body. John Gill answers that the external worship must be matched by an internal, in the exercise of every grace.

Where the psalm turns is the hard question of the entry, and it turns inside a verse. Matthew Henry says plainly that the latter part of the psalm begins in the middle of a verse, and reports that some take the clause about hearing not as a condition but as a wish, that you would hear his voice. Adam Clarke agrees and would begin the eighth verse there, since the clause opens what he takes to be the part of the priest or prophet. Keil and Delitzsch argue the grammar of it: since the verb means not merely to hear but to hear obediently, the clause cannot be the protasis of a condition at all, and where one expositor supplies an apodosis promising a blessing, they answer that the particle simply has an optative sense. Charles Ellicott resists the whole arrangement. The received version follows the old Greek in joining the clause to what comes after, but the Hebrew text connects it with the preceding half of the verse, and he sees no good reason to depart from that, since the change from the third person to the first within a single sentence would be intolerable even in this poetry, and no line need be supposed lost; he renders instead that we are the sheep of his hand, and today would that ye would hearken to his voice.

The urgency of the word today is felt by all of them alike. Adam Clarke presses it hardest: there is no time to lose, tomorrow may be too late, God calls today and tomorrow he may be silent. Matthew Henry makes hearing the voice the same thing as believing, so that if by faith the offer is accepted today it is well, but in a matter of such vast importance nothing is more dangerous than delay; and of the hardening he says that if the sinner’s heart be hardened it is his own act and deed, he hardening it himself, and he alone shall bear the blame for ever. John Wesley glosses the word as forthwith or presently. On the ground of the summons C.H. Spurgeon finds the master reason for worship in the covenant, since he is ours and therefore we will love him, and our God and therefore we will worship him. John Gill makes the same possession run both ways, and Charles Ellicott hears behind the figure the eastern custom of leading flocks by the voice. Adam Clarke notes that several of the ancient versions divide the clause otherwise, reading that we are his people and the sheep of the pasture of his hand.
8:
Charles Ellicott marks the point where the psalm changes speaker, since the mention of the guiding voice suggests to the poet that God should address his people directly, and the divine warning begins here; he adds that the two words for the place are better kept as the proper names they are. Adam Clarke and John Wesley keep them as descriptions, of a bold and wicked contest and of a day of tempting, while noting that the same two names were given to the spot. John Gill distinguishes several kinds of hardness, one natural to the corruption of our nature, one acquired by long custom in sinning, one judicial where God gives men up, and one that overtakes God’s own people through the deceitfulness of sin, of which, when they are sensible of it, they complain.

Whether the fathers knew God’s ways is answered three different ways. Adam Clarke holds that the verb to know is used here, as often elsewhere, to express approbation: they knew his ways well enough, but they did not like them and would not walk in them; they did not enter into his designs nor acknowledge what they had received. Charles Ellicott takes the opposite sense, rendering the phrase a people of wanderers in heart who are morally astray through ignorance of God’s paths, and correcting the verb of the preceding clause from grieved to loathed. John Wesley stands between, saying that after all the teaching given them they did not know, nor consider, the great things wrought for them. John Gill agrees that the word carries loathing and weariness, and reports an older commentator who dates the divine displeasure from the affair of the spies, after which nothing was heard from the mouth of the Lord nor any account given of the people until they reached the border of the land. Adam Clarke also gives his old Psalter on the same verse, that these wretched men were given to the love of this life and knew not God’s ways of meekness and charity, wherefore in his wrath he set it stably that they should not enter into his rest.

What the rest is produces the sharpest division in the chapter. Charles Ellicott says it is of course the promised land, as the context unmistakably shows, and then goes further: the freedom taken with the passage by the author of the epistle, in order to make the psalm point to a future rest, was such as the Jewish doctors ordinarily used, and other instances of the same method occur in the New Testament. Adam Clarke holds the reading Ellicott declines, that the land was a type of heaven, where after all his toils the good and faithful servant enters into the joy of his Lord, and observes that of those who came out of Egypt only two entered in, the rest dying in the wilderness through disobedience. John Wesley keeps to the promised land, which is elsewhere called the rest. John Gill attends to the oath rather than the rest, noting the form of it and that God swore by himself, since he could swear by no greater. John Gill also measures the forty years against a later period of much the same length, and Adam Clarke observes that through all those years, while the people did nothing but murmur, God seldom showed forth the judgment they had most righteously deserved.
